text:
A: Alright, boss! Can you hear me?
B: Yes, I can, thank you. Hello. I'm Martin.
A: Callum. Nice one. Sorry if it's loud, there's a nail bar under my flat and they've got the music going already.
B: Ah. I did wonder what the bass line was.
A: Every day, from nine. You get used to it, kind of. So where are you, then?
B: Lewes, in Sussex. And you're in London, I'd guess?
A: Catford, South East. Proper London, not like where I grew up out in Orpington, innit.
B: Right. I grew up in Maidstone, so I'll take your word on the distinction.
A: Ha, nah, Maidstone's fine. So what d'you do?
B: I'm a structural engineer. Mostly old bridges, and old masonry generally. People ring us when a Victorian arch has got a crack in it and they want to know whether to worry.
A: And do they have to worry?
B: Well, er, usually less than they think. Old bridges are often in better shape than they look, which is sort of the fun of it. You find odd repairs somebody made in the twenties and you try to work out what they were thinking.
A: That's actually sick, like, detective stuff.
B: That's the bit I like, yes. What about you?
A: I'm doing media and comms at uni, second year. It's basically media strategy. And I do production work on the side, events, warehouse parties, setting up rigs, lights, sound, all that.
B: That sounds like quite hard work.
A: Nah, it's a laugh, mostly. Long nights, though. The idea is music or events marketing after, running campaigns for a label or whatever. Got loads of contacts from doing it, you get me.
B: Mm. Have you got anything lined up, placements and so on?
A: Erm, not yet, not like official. It's more of a who-you-know thing in that world, innit. It'll sort itself out.
B: I'm sure. Sorry, I meant to ask, is that an Oldboy poster behind you? In your photo, I think.
A: Yes! You know Oldboy?
B: Only because my son made me watch it years ago. The corridor scene with the hammer, I think it was.
A: The corridor scene, mate! One take. People go on about it being violent, but nah, nah, see, the thing is, it's actually about guilt, the whole film. Everyone misses that.
B: That's fair. I read a lot of translated novels, and there's often that sort of thing, the story's dressed as one thing and it's really about something else entirely.
A: Exactly, that's exactly it. What've you read, then, like Korean stuff?
B: A bit. I've just finished a Han Kang, The Vegetarian. I'm not sure I understood all of it, to be honest, but I kept thinking about it for weeks.
A: See, that's the sign it's good, innit, when it stays with you.
B: I'd agree with that. Do you get much time for films, with the course and the events work?
A: Too much, if I'm honest. Watched one last night instead of doing an essay, so, you know.
B: Well, er, I've done much the same with drawings instead of reports. I won't tell anyone if you don't.
A: Deal, boss. So how long have you been doing bridges, then, like—
